title: Calder: Andrew's actual household
standfirst: Andrew’s testament names Elizat and their son Robert. The Duddingston Robert is now the preferred uncertain adult continuation, with the earlier burgh-parent pair retained as alternatives.
question: Who were Andrew's parents, and where did his named children and land pass next?
answer: Andrew's testament names wife Elizat Stevinsoun, son Robert and daughters Marion, Janet and Isobel. It names no son James, and it names no parent. Robert has a checked existing profile and a preferred uncertain Duddingston continuation; the other children’s later identities remain under review; a chronologically possible John of Glasgow is not a documented father.

chapters.title: Easter Newtoun: prefer the James father route, 40%
body: Research rationale: compare the competing childhood and father routes at the head of the largest Calder descendant branch; prefer the route with fewer unsupported identity steps while retaining compatible alternatives.

Prefer James Glasgow-991 as the possible working father of the Easter Newtoun adult John Glasgow-3610 at 40% subjective confidence, through the adult’s possible identity with John Glasgow-1084, the Mid Calder child of 1616. The 1616 index names James as father. The existing 1616-child account already carries the specific later-family attribution to Annah and the proposed 1642 Porteous marriage and 1643 Edinburgh child. The inspected 1649 and 1652 transcripts now place the named father Johne at Easter Newtoune/Easter Newtoun, supporting one adult household. This makes the existing 1616-family comparison a more economical preferred reconstruction than the 1608 route: the latter requires both the 1608 child’s identification with this adult and the identification of his named Mid Calder father with the Quothquan testator John-3296. Neither route is proved. The inherited Annah attribution is not independent corroboration of the new residence reading.

Retain John Glasgow-3296 as an unselected uncertain father alternative at 28%, through the compatible 1608 Mid Calder child. The original name, neighbouring-parish and generation argument remains viable, but its two unproved identity steps are less economical than the preferred 1616-child/James-991 route. The omission of children from the 1650 testament does not exclude him. No new record disproves the alternative.

The 40% is a combined judgement about James’s fatherhood of the later adult, not the 98% record-defined fatherhood of the 1616 child. The existing 42% childhood-to-adult comparison remains a distinct scoped assessment; these values are not independent measurements and are not mechanically multiplied. Both childhood dates fit an adult father in 1649: about 33 if baptised near birth in 1616, about 41 if in 1608. Neither childhood transcript supplies a residence, occupation or mother. The retained published Edinburgh marriage entry calls the 1642 groom a whipman but supplies no parents or residence to distinguish the candidates. The 1643 child names John and Issobell Porteous; the 1652 Annah transcript names no mother. A household, property, occupation or witness bridge to either childhood is still missing. Another local John, including the retained Linlithgow comparisons, or an unrepresented family remains possible. Robert-4006 remains a father-generation alternative. William-1087 remains a removed unsupported father, not biologically excluded merely by a 1609 baptism. John-1084 and John-3610 may be duplicate accounts, not two proved distinct sons named John; no merge is performed. Mothers remain separately assessed.

This reassessment reuses held evidence; it adds no newly inspected source. The retained Findmypast 1616 transcript reads “10 ?1616”, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.13; the supplied ScotlandsPeople index gives 18 February 1616, OPR 694/10/28. Preserve that discrepancy pending original comparison. The 1608 transcript gives 26 June, OPR 694/1 item 3 p.5. The 1649/1652 Findmypast pages, inspected on 18 October, give OPR 689/20 item 1 pp.5 and 13; supplied ScotlandsPeople references are 690/10/14 and 690/10/32. No original register was newly inspected. Repeated indexes of an event are not independent witnesses.

The selected local father changes from John-3296, uncertain 28%, to James-991, possible 40%. The previous selection and its sources remain available as an alternative. Fresh public WikiTree capture has no father attached to John-3610, so the outstanding live proposal is a new possible father, not replacement of a live father. No live edit is made. This revises the ancestry route above 309 fixed pre-1850 profile accounts (253,689 connected pairs depend on the old edge); those overlapping accounts are not 309 proved unique people. It adds no component join. Confident and supported connectivity do not increase. James’s own probable Mureistoun father, 82%, John-1084’s recorded father, 98%, Annah’s record-defined father, 96%, and John-3012’s father, 98%, retain their grades. John-3610’s before-1629 birth bound and all other vital fields and mothers are preserved.

Prioritise a discriminating household link for the Easter Newtoun adult: compare original 1649/1652 entries and their neighbours, then any 1642 marriage details, kirk-session, land or inheritance evidence tying him to James’s Mid Calder family. Test the 1608/Quothquan route in parallel. A mother or a precise holding would be more useful than another generic name match.

chapters.title: Easter Newtoun: Annah and John share the same father
body: Research rationale: test the identity alternatives in the largest Calder branch using precise household details, separating the adult father from his uncertain childhood and ancestry.

Prefer John Glasgow-3610, the adult father in the 1649 Kirknewton baptism, as Annah Glasgow-1439’s father at 96% subjective confidence. Findmypast’s transcript of John’s 22 April 1649 baptism names father Johne Glasgow and residence Easter Newtoune. Its transcript of Annah’s 20 June 1652 baptism names father Johne Glasgow and residence Easter Newtoun. The matching uncommon full paternal name, specific residence, parish and three-year interval strongly support one household. This is a combined identity inference across two child records, not a literal statement that the children were siblings. A different Johne in the same settlement or a transcription error remains possible.

The 96% concerns the record-defined father of the 1652 child and his identification with the adult father of the 1649 child. It does not identify that adult with the John baptised at Mid Calder in 1616, prove his own father, or establish Annah’s later identity as the 1676 bride. The transcripts name no mother. Issobell Porteous’s existing maternal attachment remains separately unproved; no maternity is transferred to other children. The earlier John-1084 account may represent the same adult, but its 1616-child-to-adult identity remains possible at 42%, rather than established. These are overlapping profile-identity propositions, not mutually exclusive biological fathers; the percentages must not be added or treated as independent evidence. Retain that account as an alternative and resolve the possible duplicate before any live family change. No profiles are merged.

The Findmypast transcript pages were inspected on 18 October 2026; the parish originals were not inspected. The provider gives archive OPR 689/20, item 1, pages 5 and 13, while the supplied ScotlandsPeople index gives parish 690, references 10/14 and 10/32. Preserve that reference discrepancy for original comparison. Both Findmypast pages label the place Kirknewton and East Calder. The extra indexed version of Annah’s baptism, R_686208660, also names Johne and leaves the mother blank; it is another derivative of the same event, not independent corroboration. The September daily-limit responses are historical access failures; these targeted transcript retries now succeeded, without completing the wider Findmypast audit.

The earlier household batch changed Annah’s father-profile assignment at 96%, without itself settling the adult’s ancestry. The subsequent working-ancestry review selects James-991 as possible father of John-3610 at 40%, retaining John-3296 as an unselected28% alternative; this is a separate combined inference, not an upgrade of the household evidence. John-3012’s existing 98% father role remains unchanged. All birth and death fields, mothers and saved WikiTree family fields are preserved. Margaret-3112’s competing 1646/1649 readings are unresolved: her 26 November 1649 Findmypast transcript names John and Kirknewton/East Calder, but gives no residence. It does not independently place her in the Easter Newtoun household.

Compare the original 1649 and 1652 entries, their register references and neighbouring households; look for a recorded mother, occupation or witness tying the Easter Newtoun adult to the 1642 Porteous marriage and 1616 baptism. Shared residence alone does not choose his grandparents.

chapters.title: Murieston: a probable George father for James’s large branch
body: Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule.

The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William.

The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

James’s former selected Andrew father becomes an uncertain alternative; George of Mureistoun becomes the preferred probable father. A separately uncertain William upstream link keeps the family model inspectable. The record-only George uses the existing complete sourced public subject account and is not a new WikiTree profile or an independently counted extra surname person. The 216-profile pre-1850 child side below James retains all its downstream uncertainty and possible duplicates. The working cohort’s connected components and connected pairs do not improve merely because this named intermediary is displayed. No live WikiTree save, new original inspection, mother, birth/death change or certainty upgrade is claimed.

21 October2026: the missing Berwick citation is recovered. Geo Glascoe was buried at Holy Trinity, Berwick upon Tweed, Northumberland, on 3 July 1589. The name, parish and exact date identify the existing George Glascoe-36 account. This is a burial date, not an exact death date. The transcript supplies no age, relatives or occupation; its synthetic birth-range search fields are not recorded ages or birth evidence. Scottish origin and named parentage remain unproved. The indexed burial excludes this George from the adult baptism-witness role at Mid Calder in 1605 and from the combined 1586–1605 identity. It does not exclude his being the Mureistoun man of 1586 alone. The merchant George Glasgow-1099 and George Glasgow-3171 retain their existing assessments. The selected Mureistoun George → James Glasgow-991 father remains 82%; William Glasgow-3522 → Mureistoun George remains 26%. No family link or percentage changes.

chapters.title: Fisherrow: two linked couples and the Inveresk children
body: Prefer the existing [James Glasgow](/people/glasgow-991.html) and [Christina Bie](/people/bie-55.html) family account for the Fisherrow James and Christina Bye. The printed 1624–1625 index explicitly groups James, tailor in Fisherrow and burgess of Musselburgh, his son Alexander and wife Christina Bye; it separately names Alexander’s wife Janet Clerk. Those are the same named family roles already represented by these profiles. The local James account also includes the Inveresk father sequence of 1609–1618, which can continue into the Fisherrow household. The ordinary Bye/Bie spelling and the full family fit make the identification probable, rather than a match resting only on James’s forename. This is an assessment of the preferred existing family account, not independent confirmation from its copied tree fields.

The printed sasine index places Janet Clerk with Alexander, while Christina Bye belongs with his father James. The 1637 Inveresk entry explicitly names Alexander Glasgow and Jannet Clerk as parents of their indexed son. The matching named couple and compatible 1624–1637 parish/property sequence document Alexander and Janet’s spouse relationship; no marriage ceremony date is supplied.

The Inveresk entries name Alexander Glasgow as father of Marioune in 1630, Johnne in 1632 and Bessie in 1635. They fall within the 1626–1637 series already represented by the Fisherrow Alexander’s family. The 1624–1625 sasines identify his wife Janet Clerk, and the 1637 child entry repeats that parental pair. The repeated father, parish, ordered child series and independently named couple strongly support this Alexander as the father in all three entries. This is confident family reconstruction from the combined records, not an assertion that each earlier entry names his occupation or wife.

The Mid Calder and Inveresk baptism sequences may still represent one mobile father or two contemporaries; no occupation or property recital joins them. The profile’s birth and death places remain inherited claims. The signed-in FamilySearch record VQ4V-K87 was inspected on 17 October 2026: it names William, father James and the 10 July 1614 Inveresk event, but no mother. It therefore supplies no independent evidence for Christina Bie’s maternity, consistent with the FMP and supplied ScotlandsPeople entries. The earlier citation-based claim that this record named her is withdrawn; the underlying parish image remains uninspected. Christina’s 1589 New Aberdour birth is tree-derived. Naming her as James’s wife in 1624 does not establish her as Alexander’s or William’s mother. The Andrew-3163 and Murieston-George ancestry alternatives retain their grades.

No mother is named in the three reviewed child entries, so their maternal grades stay unchanged. Bessie’s 22 March index date and existing 20 March birth field remain unreconciled; no date is changed. The later identities of these children, James-3923 versus the Edinburgh weaver James-1150, and the Edward property associations remain separate. Existing confident father settings for James-3923, Robert-1149 and Allexander-1152 are retained, not counted as new upgrades. Original sasines and parish images were not newly inspected.

Six existing assessments are strengthened: Alexander’s father and James’s Christina spouse identity become probable; Alexander and Janet’s marriage is documented; three previously ungraded fathers become strongly supported. The four paternal grade changes enter the probable-or-stronger graph, three of them the confident graph. No person, parent ID, maternal grade, date, selected working parent or live certainty flag changes. The existing pre-1850 child side below Alexander contains 24 profile accounts; downstream uncertainty remains explicit.

chapters.title: The 1673 Kirknewton Alexander: a probable local father
body: Alexander’s 1673 Kirknewton birth/baptism index explicitly names father Alexander Glasgow. The existing Alexander-3118 account is the same-parish man indexed marrying Margaret Smith in 1667, six years earlier, with a compatible father generation and a later Agnes child association in 1677. The exact father name, parish and ordered household chronology together favour that existing adult as the named father. Assess the attachment as probable rather than leaving it ungraded. This is an inference identifying the indexed father with the 1667 adult; the child entry alone does not identify that adult by wife, trade or property.

Another Alexander could have fathered the 1673 child. The marriage and baptism supply no inspected cross-reference, and the father’s circa-1650 birth is an estimate, not an age statement. Margaret Smith is not named as mother in the reviewed 1673 entry and receives no maternity upgrade. Andrew-1546 remains an uncertain proposed son of the older Alexander. Alexander-1141 remains an unproved child of the 1673 Alexander; the latter himself remains a possible older father behind the 1721–1732 child series. The 1673 birth/baptism dates, the 1701 and 1705 marriages and the later children’s maternity questions are retained. The older John-3610 father route is not strengthened.

chapters.title: Duddingston’s Robert: the Corsoun household as preferred uncertain parents
body: Current 23 October 2026: This regrades the existing James-1150 to Robert-1156 pair only, from 86% probable to 91% confident inference. It names no new father. Robert’s own Andrew-3163 father hypothesis stays 28%; Elizat’s and Deborah’s maternal conclusions are unchanged. The Duffe adult identification remains 70% and James-2682’s conditional Robert father remains 61%; these subjective nested assessments are not recalculated by multiplication. All people, life dates and other family links remain separate. No live WikiTree edit is made. On 23 October 2026 the signed-in FamilySearch catalogue identified Duddingston OPR 684 volumes 1–8, catalogue koha:31948. Preferred film 1066684/DGS 007908839 includes the 1631–1667 burials; alternative film 103022/DGS 008059362 includes the same period. Both normal viewers displayed “Unable to Display Image Group” and denied permission to share it. This is a custodial-access limit, not a missing record, a sign-in problem or negative genealogy. Seek OPR 684/60/47 through normal authorized ScotlandsPeople access or a custodian/library copy; do not repeat the same blocked film lookup.

The preferred local working parents of the Duddingston Robert are now Andrew Glasgow and Elizat Stevinsoun, through possible identity with their recorded son Robert-4006. The accepted 1597/8 testament expressly names Robert as Andrew’s son by Elizat and makes provision until he reached age. A minor then can fit the adult generation of the Robert buried at Duddingston in 1647 and the confidently inferred father (91%) of James the Edinburgh weaver. The retained circa-1582 and 1597/before-1597 dates are estimates or bounds, not two exact birth records in conflict. On the maintained, queried Calder-area reading of Andrew’s residence, this offers a positive named-child family candidate in the relevant broad Lothian comparison. The earlier Archibald/Isobell pair has no record naming the Duddingston Robert as its child. Prefer the recorded Corsoun family as the uncertain route, with both former parents retained as alternatives.

The 1598 child and the Duddingston adult remain separate WikiTree profiles with an uncertain identity comparison; no merge is inferred. No holding, occupation, wife or named-relative bridge equates them, and the Corsoun/Calder place reading itself remains queried. A different local Robert, including the separate Ninian-son account Robert-1027, remains a comparison. Ninian’s son keeps his proved parents and is not conflated with Andrew’s named son. Elizat’s maternity is direct for the recorded child only; it is uncertain for the Duddingston adult because it depends on the same identity hypothesis. Archibald’s and Isobell’s biological parentage is not disproved. James-1150’s separately reassessed 91% confident father inference, all other selected families, and the adult’s existing vital fields remain unchanged. Two modern Robert accounts can represent one historical son; they are not independent evidence for two sons.

One paternal and one maternal working choice are replaced, affecting a child side of 64 pre-1850 profiles. This improves the source basis of the preferred route, without raising either adult parent link above uncertain. Existing live parent fields and flags remain unchanged. The record-son’s already-confident father is reaffirmed, while Elizat’s recorded motherhood and the Andrew–Elizat spouse relationship receive formal documented assessments. The main view also reconciles already-completed profile redirects and the previously corrected public 1598 household; these are publication repairs, not new historical people or newly discovered records.

Historical source test, 22 October 2026 (superseded for the older James’s father grade on 23 October): the printed 1641 apprenticeship was reread and all 21 displayed results in a surname-only, exact 1647 Findmypast Parish Burials search were enumerated. None identified the Duddingston entry; most were undated monumental-inscription hits, so this is not an absence claim. The original 1647 burial remains the next discriminating record. Robert’s fatherhood of the Edinburgh weaver stays 86%; Andrew’s Corsoun father link stays 28%, while Elizat’s selected mother link remains uncertain and individually unrated. No relationship grade or family membership changes. See Robert’s current research account for the exact search scope.

chapters.title: Calder and Irvine: selected uncertain parent families
body: Kirknewton review, 20 October 2026: the 1681 William/Marion banns couple is selected at 69%, and Marion-3025 is preferred as Bessie-1545’s possible mother at 54%. Ann McCook’s former confident tree flag is retained in the review and downgraded locally for Bessie only. This does not identify the mother of the 1702 John, prove the Meek adult’s childhood, or strengthen William-1026’s own 24% John-3610 father. The other Calder/Irvine parent hypotheses retain their grades. [Current household and alternatives](/people/glasgow-1545.html#research-findings).

Select William Glasgow-1026 as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3481, the combined Calder father account recorded in 1730 and with Christian Meek in 1751–1755. This adopts possible identity with John Glasgow-1544, the child indexed at Kirknewton in 1702 with father William. The same name and parish and a normal adult generation favour this concrete child account over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1702, he would be about 28 in 1730 and 53 at the 1755 child. Those ages are conditional examples, not ages stated in the registers. The old circa 1710 birth was inferred from assumed age at the 1730 fatherhood and cannot exclude the 1702 child. The child’s existing father identity as William-1026 is itself qualified; no record explicitly identifies the later Meek husband as his son.

John-1544 and John-3481 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selection does not establish two distinct John sons. The 1702 date remains unreconciled: the child’s field uses a before 11 November boundary while its biography cites a 29 November baptism. Neither date is newly corrected. The later account combines the 1730 father of Jean, whose mother is omitted, with the 1751 and 1755 Meek household. That earlier adult identification remains a preferred working combination, not a continuous household proved by occupation, land or witnesses. John-81, estimated born 1709, remains a specific competing identity for the 1730 father. His Guthrie household is indexed with children in West Calder in 1751 and 1753 while the Meek household appears in Kirknewton in 1751 and Leith in 1755. That concrete overlap makes a simple succession of wives less persuasive; do not combine the full Guthrie and Meek families without resolving the entries. No birth estimate alone excludes John-81. Other local John origins remain possible. Ann McCook is not selected as John-3481’s mother: the reviewed 1702 child citation names William, and the attached Ann field does not supply an independently verified maternal clause. William’s existing uncertain John-3610 father and older family alternatives retain their grades; no date or family field is changed to force the new route.

Select John Glasgow-1057 and Agnes Spark-330 as the uncertain working parents of George Glasgow-4165, father with Margt at Irvine in 1741–1745. The preferred model uses possible identity with their son George Glasgow-1058, baptised at Kilwinning on 20 November 1687 and already associated with the George/Margaret Martain couple indexed marrying there on 11 June 1728. That couple’s son George-3312 is indexed at Kilwinning in 1729. The nearby Irvine household later repeats George and Margt, with no maternal surname or father’s age stated. This offers a specific existing couple and a compatible continuation across neighbouring parishes. On an infant-baptism assumption, the elder George would be about 54–58 at the Irvine children; late fatherhood remains possible. Margaret’s circa 1704 estimate would fit an adult mother in 1741–1745, but it is only a marriage-derived estimate. Neither calculation proves the identities or a move.

Agnes Spark’s proposed maternity is assessed independently from the same positive child evidence: the 1687 baptism index explicitly names John Glasgow and Agnes Spark as George’s parents. Their already confident parentage for the recorded child is not newly upgraded. Transferring either parent to the Irvine adult depends on the uncertain child/groom/Irvine identity chain, so both new adult links remain uncertain. They share that premise and are correlated, not independent confirmations. Margt in the 1741–1745 entries is George’s co-parent, not evidence for his own mother; Margaret Martin is not assigned a new mother or merged with any other Margaret.

The 1687 child, 1728 groom and Irvine father may be different men. The match of Margt to Margaret Martin is compatible, not a full recorded maternal surname match, and no age, occupation or property bridges the two parishes. The existing 1687-child/1728-adult family account also needs its identity assessment kept separate from the child’s explicit parent clause. A younger George from the Irvine Hugh/Service, James/Rae or another local family remains possible. The proposed father James-4158 would give a normal generation if George was born around 1720, but no record names him as George’s father; the specific older George/Margaret household is preferred provisionally. Keep the merchant son George-3312 distinct. If his 1729 entry represents infant baptism, he would be only about 12 at the 1741 fatherhood, a strong objection to assigning those children directly to that son. The index event type and adult-child identities still require their own review; an unsupported older birth estimate must not decide them. No merchant trade, Nethermains ownership, Manchester patent or artillery career is transferred to the Irvine father. No identity merge, duplicate removal or live relationship save is performed.

Two selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother using existing parish and profile research. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. John’s new mother remains unknown. Existing dates, recorded couples, earlier uncertain routes and possible duplicate accounts are retained; connectivity measures profile accounts, not proved distinct individuals.

Select Johne Glasgow-3093, indexed at Mid Calder in 1648 as son of Jamis Glasgow, as the very low-confidence working father of Robert Glasgow-4168, father at Libberton in 1718–1726. The preferred local route runs through Johne’s existing uncertain James-3332 father identity and that James’s possible identification with the Lindsaylands weaver indexed in 1680. Lindsaylands and Quothquan/Libberton supply the adjacent Lanarkshire family setting; Mid Calder is a separate parish and no migration is proved. A Johne born around 1648 could father Robert in the 1680s–1690s, allowing ordinary adult fatherhood at the 1718 baptism. This generation is preferred over assigning Robert directly to the older weaver, who was dead by 1680 if that identity is correct. It is a specific family hypothesis using recorded men, not a father clause in Robert’s records.

Johne’s only reviewed record is the 1648 child entry; no later occupation, residence, spouse or death identifies him with Libberton. The Jamis-to-Glasgow-3332 identity and the latter’s Lindsaylands identity are both uncertain. Its inherited circa 1634 birth would make him only about fourteen at Johne’s 1648 event if literal; that unsourced estimate must not establish or exclude parentage. The 1648 source names Jamis, not John-1084. The known parish association therefore belongs to a conditional family chain, not to an independently followed migration. Agnes’s maternity is assessed separately: the 1675 FamilySearch parent index explicitly identifies Agnes Eastone in Thomas Glesgow’s entry, while John is named as father in the paired child citation. This is a positive maternal source for that child, not merely John’s spouse field. Agnes’s attachment to the Clarkson adult remains uncertain because the child/adult identity is uncertain. The preferred model treats the two early Quothquan men as paternal brothers rather than making the later John James’s father. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. This uses a named family already connected to Quothquan, at very low confidence, rather than inventing a missing parent. No record names Stephen as James’s father or James and John as brothers.

The route depends both on the proposed James–John brotherhood and on John’s already uncertain Stephen parentage. The Glasgow–Montfoid–Mid Calder–Quothquan identities are not proved migrations. John’s 1650 testament names his sister Bessie and no child or parent; omission of James, already dead by 1624, does not disprove brotherhood. John himself could instead be James’s father if older than his inherited estimate, or the men could be uncle/nephew, cousins or unrelated local namesakes. The older John and Thomas tenants in the 1520s–1530s remain possible ancestral relatives with unproved intervening generations; no direct father edge to them is selected. This adopts an existing comparison in the captured child profile, rather than inventing a new named parent from the marriage alone. Exact forename and surname, the compatible Lothian setting and an age of about twenty in 1632 if baptised near birth favour this childhood as a practical working choice. The child’s baptism names David, but neither it nor the marriage supplies the bridge between child and adult. Shared name and compatible chronology do not prove the identity. Prefer this young-adult explanation provisionally over an older widow or an unrecorded childhood, at low confidence.

Retain Glasgow-1085 and Glasgow-3185 as separate profile accounts of a possible single woman; the selected parent does not establish two distinct daughters called Issobell. The father–daughter link is already confidently marked for the record-defined 1612 child; only the transfer to the 1632 bride is newly selected and uncertain. The marriage index names no father, age, birthplace, prior marital status or children. The 19 July date belongs to a combined banns/marriages index and is not newly verified as the ceremony date. The bride’s before-1612 birth boundary is an inferred profile estimate, not a birth record or an independently established exclusion of the May 1612 child. It is retained unchanged; no new birth date is entered to force the connection. The child’s 1642 Hardington, Somerset death fields remain an unsourced tree-held later-life lead in this review, not a verified fate or proof of migration. Even if correct, that later date alone would not exclude the 1632 marriage. The older Isobel Glasgow-3336, who represents Andrew’s testament-named daughter and is probably the William Symountoun bride of 1619 and mother of the 1620 child, remains a possible remarriage alternative. No death of Symountoun, remarriage record or continuing incompatible household was inspected; do not exclude her merely because she already has a spouse. An unrecorded Isobel remains possible and the candidate list is not exhaustive. No mother is named in the 1612 baptism review, so none is selected for the bride. David’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and supplies no independent corroboration. Existing relatives, dates and all confidently marked links are preserved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Working connectivity counts the retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Campbeltown: a provisional Linlithgow origin and Agnes’s placement
body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. A child baptised in 1622 could have been about 37 at Alexander’s 1659 Campbeltown event and about 28 in the approximate 1650 generation assigned to James and Agnes. This is a workable adult generation for the household. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

Select George Glasgow-3100 as Agnes Glasgow-1562’s uncertain working father. This activates the existing geographic family suggestion: Agnes’s captured profile places her Longwill household in Campbeltown, with a 1670 marriage-year field and a son’s 1683 birth field, while George is the named father in the 1659 Campbeltown event. Their approximate parent/child generations permit an older daughter in that household. The same locality and generation make daughter a useful provisional placement alongside George’s attached James and recorded Alexander. The marriage year, child details and Agnes’s circa-1650 birth are profile-held leads, not a newly inspected parish entry. No source names Agnes’s father; a sister, cousin, other local family or unrecorded father remains possible.

George-1560 and George-3100 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; shared proposed parentage does not prove two distinct sons called George or an identity merge. The 1605 and 1627 childhood candidates remain viable, and the list is not exhaustive. A separate unrecorded childhood is possible. The illustrative ages assume baptism near birth. George-3100’s 1630 structured and 1640 narrative births are unsupported estimates; neither is silently replaced by a proved 1622 birth. The existing John review cites X1RN-XV7 whereas the child profile cites X1RN-XVQ; retain that reference difference for original-register comparison, without treating the citations as independent events. James-1496’s father link to George is inherited and unproved; its name pattern supplies no independent corroboration for the chosen childhood. Agnes’s 1670 marriage field does not establish her age. No birth year is altered to force a generation. Assess mothers separately. No mother is supplied for the 1622 child in this review and none is selected for the Campbeltown adult. Grizel Dunlop-3562 is already the confidently marked mother of Alexander-3101 in the 1659 event, but that does not establish her maternity of Agnes or James. Her circa-1640 birth is also an unsupported estimate. Neither James nor Agnes receives a mother. The FMP 13 April 1659 birth-date field and Scotland’s People 12 April index date remain literal alternatives; the original entry and reference conventions are unresolved. The Auchinhork residence reading is not assigned a guessed modern place. John-1561’s own Andrew-of-Calder father and his other childhood-to-adult comparisons remain uncertain. No new original inspection, confident relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and retains the possible duplicate.

chapters.title: Three more early family placements, explicitly uncertain
body: The local working tree now selects William of Saltmarket as Michael of Stevenston’s possible father, Andrew of Calder as Jonat Menzeis’s possible father, and Ninian as Barbara Wilson’s possible father. These choices use the existing brother/cousin, same-parish remarriage and daughter/niece comparisons.

Michael Glasgow of Stevenston: The existing Stevenston study places Michael as a probable brother or cousin of James elder of Corsankell, rather than his son. Michael was an adult witness in the Glencairn estate network in 1549; both appear in the same small estate landscape in the 1559–60 teind list. Their approximate 1525 and 1515 generations fit brothers. Select the brother option provisionally and extend James’s already uncertain father William to Michael. This uses an existing older household without inventing an intervening person. The Mathie–Glencairn network supplies a credible route between the burgh family and these estates. Limits: The brother-versus-cousin choice is unresolved, and James’s own father William is uncertain. No record calls Michael William’s son. A cousin through another burgh household, an older generation than the estimated 1525 birth, or a separate family remains possible. Brakpleuch and Dubbs may represent one Michael or two. No mother, exact birth or death is inferred.

Jonat Glasgow, wife of David Menzeis: Jonat is the mother in a Mid Calder baptism in 1609. The existing comparison prefers her possible identity with Jonet Glasgow who married Martin Ramsy in the same parish in 1624, fifteen years later. That Jonet is already placed as Andrew’s testament daughter. Select Andrew as Jonat’s uncertain father through this local identity reconstruction. Her estimated 1585 generation fits Andrew’s household; the same name, parish and feasible remarriage sequence favour this model over the more distant Ninian household. Limits: This combines two uncertain identity steps: the 1609 mother with the 1624 bride, and the bride with Andrew’s testament daughter. David Menzeis’s death and the bride’s widowhood are not recorded in the material reviewed. Jonat and Jonet may be different women; retain both profiles and do not count an identity merge. Ninian Glasgow remains a competing father hypothesis. No mother is attached.

Barbara Glasgow, wife of Johne Wilsoune: The existing branch assessment already favours Barbara as a daughter or niece of Ninian. Her 1611 South Leith marriage entry fits the Leith setting of Ninian’s possible son William and the adjoining Edinburgh craft households; Ninian’s documented son Robert was a cordiner. The estimated 1590 daughter generation fits Ninian’s estimated 1550 generation. Select daughter as the simpler working placement within this already identified household, while retaining niece as an alternative. This is a combined locality, generation and family-network inference. Limits: Neither the marriage entry nor Ninian’s testament names Barbara as his daughter. The proposed Leith brother William is himself uncertain, and shared craft geography is suggestive rather than individual proof. Barbara may instead be Ninian’s niece or belong to another local family. If she is Barbara-567, the existing William-3522 father claim becomes a rival explanation. The adult Barbara identities remain separate, the 1611 date discrepancy stays open, and no mother is assigned.

Each is low confidence and counts only as a selected uncertain parent in the working graph. Keep possible duplicate profiles separate, mothers independent, and the confident graph unchanged. No new source reading is claimed.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: Assessment history: the 17 October Murieston preferred-father review above supersedes the earlier selection of Andrew as James’s father. George of Mureistoun is now preferred, probable; Andrew remains an uncertain alternative. The earlier source readings and limits below are retained.

The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.
